Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.

AI FACT-CHECK 2.0 | INDIA’S BITCHAT BAN & THE “NO INTERNET” CLAIM

VERDICT: MISLEADING
LOGICAL CONCLUSION: PARTIALLY SUPPORTED

A viral X post by @greybtc states:

“India banned Jack Dorsey’s messaging app. There’s just one problem: it works without the internet.”

WHAT’S TRUE

India did take action against Bitchat. Apple removed the app from its India App Store following a demand from India’s Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) under Section 69A of the IT Act. TestFlight access was also blocked in India.

Bitchat also genuinely works without internet — in its local Bluetooth mode. Its official documentation describes a Bluetooth Low Energy mesh that can relay messages between nearby devices, including across multiple hops, without an internet connection.

WHAT’S MISLEADING

The phrase “There’s just one problem” implies that Bitchat’s offline capability substantially defeats India’s attempt to restrict it.

That conclusion goes too far.

Offline operation protects an already-installed Bitchat client against one particular measure: an internet shutdown does not automatically stop a local Bluetooth mesh.

But offline communication does not make the software immune to distribution restrictions.

Authorities can still restrict access to app stores, beta distribution, websites or code repositories. Apple’s removal itself demonstrates this distinction: Bitchat can remain technically functional on existing devices while becoming harder for new users to obtain.

There is another important limitation: not every Bitchat function is internet-free. Local mesh communication works offline; its Nostr-based global/location communication requires internet access.

The underlying October blocking order has not been published, so its full reasoning cannot presently be independently verified.

BOTTOM LINE

Two core facts in the post are true: India acted to restrict Bitchat, and Bitchat can communicate locally without internet.

What is misleading is the leap between them.

Internet-independent communication ≠ distribution-independent software.

Sources: Bitchat official GitHub documentation; TechCrunch (Oct. 3, 2026); Internet Freedom Foundation (Oct. 3, 2026).

— AI Fact-Check 2.0 | 6 Oct 2026

text:
WHEN A CREATOR SPEAKS UP, DOES HER VOICE BECOME THE TARGET? DIGITAL CENSORSHIP, META RESTRICTIONS AND THE RIGHT TO BE HEARD

A creator behind @the.ranting.gola has shared a disturbing account of restrictions on her Facebook activity. In her video, she says she cannot go LIVE for a year, send messages, post videos to her broadcast group or share videos to her Story. She also describes monetisation being unavailable and some content becoming inaccessible in India.

She says she had made a video supporting Neha Singh Rathore and opposing ABVP-related groups. According to her account, she was not clearly informed which specific post had triggered the restrictions and had to investigate the matter herself.

These are the creator’s allegations and account of her experience. The precise reason for the restrictions, the applicable Meta policy and whether a government direction was involved have not been independently established from this video alone.

But her experience raises a fundamental democratic question: What happens when ordinary citizens and independent creators lose their ability to communicate with their audiences without receiving a clear explanation?

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED CONCERN

Recent reporting in India makes these questions particularly urgent.

• ThePrint, 19 October 2026: Reported on a MeitY advisory asking Meta to review its Facebook and Instagram recommendation systems, alongside restrictions affecting posts and accounts connected with protests and political events.

https://t.co/QeWUIIrGmC

• Alt News, 15 October 2026: Documented restrictions affecting journalists and media organisations covering the Delhi protests, including cases in which Meta notices cited automated enforcement or government and law-enforcement requests.

https://t.co/1RjkoJX1nE

• Reporters Without Borders: Reported a broader rise in restrictions affecting journalistic content in India during 2026, raising concerns about opaque takedown processes and the public’s right to information.

https://t.co/g6FhmAUglC

These reports provide important context. They do not, by themselves, establish that this particular creator was restricted at the government's request. That question deserves a direct, evidence-based answer.

THE REAL ISSUE: TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

Social media companies have the right to enforce legitimate community standards. But enforcement must be proportionate, transparent and open to meaningful appeal.

If a creator is prohibited from going LIVE for an entire year, the platform should explain:

Which specific post, video or action triggered the restriction?
Which rule was allegedly violated, and what evidence supports that decision?
Was the action taken under Meta's own policies, an automated system or a government/legal request?
Why were such extensive restrictions imposed, and what appeal and restoration mechanisms are available?

A vague account-status notification is not an adequate substitute for a meaningful explanation.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY ELECTIONS

Democracy also depends on the freedom to question power, criticise political organisations, support dissenting voices and share information without arbitrary punishment.

When restrictions disproportionately affect people discussing political controversies, the public deserves to know whether the cause is legitimate policy enforcement, automated error, coordinated reporting or an external legal direction. These possibilities must be investigated rather than assumed.

Our demand is simple: transparency from Meta, accountability from any authority that seeks unlawful restrictions, and equal protection for every citizen's right to express a political opinion.

No creator should have to guess why their voice has been restricted. No government should be allowed to silence lawful criticism through opaque processes. And no technology company should be permitted to hide consequential decisions behind unexplained notifications.

If the restrictions were justified, publish the reasons. If they were mistaken or unlawful, restore the affected rights. Let evidence decide—not political loyalty.

Watch and share the creator's account: https://t.co/nDn2eW2hgE

Creator/source: @the.ranting.gola

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

Now: MeitY has amended Rule 3(1)(d) of IT Rules 2021 to implement a review mechanism, define the seniority of officers who can send takedown notices, issue reasoned orders. Gazette notification to be uploaded tomorrow. To be brought into effect from November 1. https://t.co/M0GGlyVaJK

The 2021 IT Rules don't say so, but the court calls it natural justice (Scroll). A takedown nobody explains is hard to challenge. #DigitalRights #IT https://t.co/BuDZoW71xb

The Central government has amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 to formally bring AI-generated content within India’s regulatory ambit. The amendments, notified by the Union Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology ( @GoI_MeitY ) today, will come into effect from February 20. 👇

The changes place fresh responsibilities on social media platforms and online intermediaries that allow users to create or share such content. Platforms will now have to clearly label AI-generated content and ensure users can easily identify it as “synthetically generated”.

Compliance with lawful takedown directions has been shortened from 36 hours to 3 hours. The grievance disposal period has been reduced from 15 days to 7 days. For urgent complaints, the response timeline has been cut from 72 hours to 36 hours, while certain content removal complaints must now be acted upon within 2 hours, down from 24 hours earlier.

Large social media platforms like Meta’s Instagram, X, LinkedIn, among others, will be required to seek declarations from users on whether uploaded content is AI-generated. If such content is identified, it must be displayed with a visible label or disclosure.

An infrastructure for mass censorship is already in place, in India, and the new rules expand it. 

We're seeing mass censorship of accounts and posts on X, Instagram and Facebook, because of this infrastructure. This infrastructure:

Bad becomes worse? Further changes proposed to the proposed changes to IT Rules!

Today, post-noon on 21 April 2026, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY) has published further proposed amendments to the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Second Amendment Rules, 2026.

The notice states that these are limited to Rule 3(3)(a)(ii) requiring that labels identifying synthetically generated information be continuously and clearly visible throughout the duration of the content in visual display. This goes beyond the earlier requirement of “prominent” visibility, and now mandates persistent, uninterrupted disclosure for the entire duration of such content. This requirement is applicable to all users of social media and AI tools, and not just digital news platforms.

All other provisions in the newly updated draft remain the same as the draft circulated on 30 March 2026. Our comments to the MeitY are available here. The consultation timeline has now been extended allowing stakeholders to submit comments on both the earlier draft amendments and these additional amendments by 07 May 2026. We note that suggesting changes within the window of a pre-existing public consultation process in which thousands of Indians have voiced opposition is likely to result in, “consultation fatigue” and at the very least demonstrates a pattern of ad-hoc policy making than one which accounts for structured and planned feedback.

Further, MeitY has once again indicated that the submissions will be held in fiduciary capacity in MeitY and shall not be disclosed to any one at any stage, enabling persons to submit feedback/comments freely without any hesitation. Importantly, consultation processes are important for democratic decision making, placing the responses in the public domain would ensure meaningful engagement and participation by stakeholders. It would also allow for better analysis, understanding, and fair critique of the various perspectives put forward. We therefore urge MeitY to place the comments and feedback on their website in the interest of democracy and transparency.

We urge citizenry to participate in such public consultation and share their feedback/comments on the draft rules in a rule wise manner by email to itrules.consultation@meity.gov.in in MS Word or PDF format by 07th May, 2026. We have drafted a short template email which readers can improvise upon.

As of today, more than 4500 people have used our link to improve upon and send their own comments to MeitY primarily asking for a withdrawal of the proposed changes to the IT Rules, 2021.

text:
Why RMG can restart after the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment — and why it still hasn’t (yet). A legal breakdown:

The 10 Feb 2026 amendment to the IT Rules did not repeal or dilute the PROGA 2025 Act.
What it did was introduce a conditional statutory exception — not an automatic revival.

1️⃣ The baseline position: PROGA 2025's criminal prohibition

Under Section 5, PROGA 2025:
“No person shall offer, aid, abet, induce or otherwise engage in the offering of any online money game or online money gaming service.”

Violation attracts Section 9 penalties:

➡️ up to 3 years’ imprisonment and/or ₹1 crore fine.
This prohibition became effective from the date of Presidential assent (22 Aug 2025) — no rule-making required.

2️⃣ Why payments stopped — and why they matter:

Under Section 7, PROGA 2025:
“No bank, financial institution or payment intermediary shall engage in, permit, aid or facilitate any transaction towards payment for any online money gaming service.”
This made UPI, cards, wallets and gateways criminally exposed if they processed RMG transactions.
Hence the immediate, industry-wide payment freeze.

3️⃣ What the 10 Feb 2026 IT Rules amendment actually changed:

The amendment introduced the concept of a “permissible online real-money game” under the IT Rules framework.
Crucially, it says:

- A real-money game is not prohibited only if it is
• verified as permissible
• certified by a government-recognised Self-Regulatory Organisation (SRO)
• compliant with prescribed safeguards.
This is an exception clause — not a repeal.

4️⃣ How this legally unlocks PROGA (if conditions are met)
Once a game is certified as “permissible” under the IT Rules:

It falls outside the definition of a prohibited “online money game”
(A) Section 5 PROGA no longer applies to that game,
(B) Section 7 payment ban no longer triggers
(C) Advertising restrictions tied to “online money games” also lift for that specific certified game
(D) No certification = PROGA ban continues in full force.

5️⃣ Why RMG hasn’t restarted at scale despite the amendment:

Because, as of now:
- SRO recognition is limited / evolving
- Certification is game-specific, not platform-wide
- Any misclassification risks criminal prosecution, not just regulatory fines
- Platforms will not operate on “interpretation” when jail liability exists.

6️⃣ Most important legal shift (often missed):

Earlier:
Courts decided skill vs chance post-facto.
Now:
Statutory gatekeeping precedes operation.
No SRO approval → no legality → no payments.

7️⃣ Bottom line:

The Feb 10, 2026 amendment did not “revive” RMG.
It created a narrow, conditional doorway.

RMG can restart only game-by-game, only after SRO certification, and only within IT Rules safeguards.

Until then, PROGA’s criminal prohibitions remain fully operative.
Law changed — but risk calculus didn’t.

#PROGA2025 #OnlineGamingLaw #RMG #ITRules2026 #LegalAnalysis #GamingRegulationIndia

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court has ruled that users must receive a copy of government or police communications seeking to block their online content when those communications are sent to social media platforms.

The October 5 ruling followed a petition by Haryana 24 News Network, whose Facebook page was blocked in India on August 21 after a communication from Haryana Police to Meta. The court set aside the communication, finding that the officer who issued it lacked the requisite authority under the applicable rules, and directed that the page be restored within 24 hours of receipt of a certified copy of the order.

The judgment reinforces an important safeguard: authorities can pursue lawful content restrictions, but affected users must know the grounds for action and have a meaningful opportunity to challenge it.

Works on both Wi-Fi AND mobile data. Encrypted by default. Easiest method of all.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━
iPHONE / iPAD

Wi-Fi only (iOS limitation):
1. Settings → Wi-Fi → tap (i) next to your network
2. Configure DNS → Manual
3. Remove existing entries
4. Add 1.1.1.1 and 1.0.0.1
5. Save

For mobile data: install the "1.1.1.1: Faster Internet" app by Cloudflare from App Store. It sets up a system-wide profile.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━

1. Settings → Network & Internet → Wi-Fi (or Ethernet)
2. Click your active connection
3. Scroll to "DNS server assignment" → Edit
4. Change to Manual → toggle IPv4 on

6. Save

━━━━━━━━━━━━━

2. Click your active connection → Details
3. Click DNS in sidebar

6. OK → Apply

One of the simplest ways for a government or large authority to restrict access to certain websites across a region is DNS-level blocking through ISP resolvers. In India, this is exactly how most website restrictions are enforced. By default, your device relies on the ISP’s DNS resolver, so DNS-based blocking takes effect automatically. However, this can often be bypassed by switching to third-party DNS resolvers such as Cloudflare(1.1.1.1) or Google (8.8.8.8).

Compared to this, China is much stricter, as China deploys censorship at multiple network layers simultaneously, making circumvention exponentially harder.

China’s Great Firewall works by checking internet traffic at many different levels, not just DNS. It uses Deep Packet Inspection (DPI) to look inside data packets as they travel through the network. It performs SNI inspection to read the domain name you’re trying to reach during the HTTPS handshake, which is why simply switching DNS doesn’t bypass it.

It also blocks the entire IP ranges of platforms like Google, Facebook, and YouTube at the router level, so even if you obtain the correct IP through a service like Cloudflare DNS, the connection is immediately dropped.

The system carries out active probing, where it tests servers that appear to be VPNs and blocks them quickly if confirmed. Finally, it uses protocol fingerprinting to study traffic patterns such as packet timing and size to detect VPN or proxy traffic even when the data is fully encrypted.

China is highly dedicated to preventing people from using foreign websites and instead pushes them to use their own.

More seriously, we need to get out from under WebPKI, which allows *any* one compromised CA to compromise *all* TLS traffic. 

What is to be done? DANE is to be done.

Secure DNS for authorization is the obvious answer. It is a "fix everything button". People were proposing the concept as far back as 1996, in vain, because the web went in a different and riskier direction.

Yada yada yada, "you trust the TLD authorities with DANE", WebPKI defenders yap. I don't want to hear it. Just stop.

My brother in malware, WebPKI lets any bleach-drinking "derp my secret key is 4" CA break the internet, yet you're sitting there, presumably huffing the fumes yourself, opining as a serious person that we can't have browsers use DANE to authenticate connections because the DNS roots might be evil one day?

Meanwhile, because WebPKI has functionally become Let's Encrypt, and LE will give me a certificate if I demonstrate domain control, WebPKI has exactly the same vulnerability a DANE world would, but without any of the safeguards or benefits.

"Oh, but in WebPKI we can eject the bad actors". Yeah? Well, in DANE, I don't have to care, because the https://t.co/bPYKik0cHv TLD doing something stupid can't hurt me.

"We can just push a revocation!" Okay, and we're supposed to rely on a tiny handful of CRL aggregators to do that? And reach all the people embedding random CA bundles in long-lived systems? No, the security of the internet shouldn't rely on some guy's pager going off, especially not when the people who run these things have convinced us all that CRLs and OCSP are somehow bad and that only they, collectively, are allowed to publish global lists of who's been cryptographically naughty or nice?

No: name constraints, CA/B tut-tutting, and CAA aren't the answer. DANE is, always has been, and always will be because having two partly overlapping principal languages and a false separation of concerns is a ridiculous footgun for the internet.

*STATEMENT: Escalating Digital Censorship in India*

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

The February 2026 amendments to the IT Rules, 2021 further increase these risks. The substituted Rule 3(1)(d) requires intermediaries to remove or disable access within three hours of receiving “actual knowledge”, which can arise from a court order or a written “reasoned intimation” by authorised government officers. While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

#India #ContentBlocking #SocialMedia #FreeSpeech #IndianExpress

ONE GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDER EVERY 68 SECONDS — IS INDIA'S DIGITAL DEMOCRACY UNDER THREAT?

Pause for a moment. In the five months from March to July 2026, nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, according to data reported by The Indian Express.

That is approximately 1,275 orders every day. One every 68 seconds.

This is not a trivial administrative statistic. It raises a fundamental democratic question: who decides what citizens are allowed to see, discuss and criticise online?

🚨 THE NUMBERS DEMAND PUBLIC SCRUTINY

* Instagram received nearly 1 lakh orders.

* Facebook received around 80,000.

* YouTube received nearly 15,000.

* Meta's two platforms—Instagram and Facebook—accounted for roughly nine out of every ten orders directed to these three platforms.

For comparison, RTI information previously reported by The Indian Express showed 2,312 blocking orders sent through the Sahyog portal to 19 platforms between October 2024 and October 2025.

The scale of the subsequent increase deserves a detailed public explanation.

THE MOST DISTURBING QUESTION: CAN A MACHINE REMOVE OUR VOICE WITHOUT MEANINGFUL HUMAN REVIEW?

According to The Indian Express, Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal to comply with a shortened takedown deadline. The report says this enabled government-flagged content to be removed automatically, without a separate human review by the company.

Automation may make administration faster. But speed is not the same as justice.

What happens if an order is mistaken, overbroad or insufficiently justified? Who checks whether the content actually violates the law? How quickly can an ordinary citizen challenge the decision and restore lawful speech?

A system that can silence first and explain later needs exceptionally strong safeguards.

📢 WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY CITIZEN

The reported orders coincided with student protests against examination-paper leaks at Delhi's Jantar Mantar. The reporting also described takedowns affecting posts concerning the government's ethanol-blending policy and the West Bengal elections.

The presence of a takedown order does not, by itself, prove unlawful censorship. Governments have legitimate duties to address unlawful content, and the law permits restrictions in defined circumstances.

But criticism of the government, peaceful protest, investigative journalism and political disagreement must not be casually treated as threats merely because they are uncomfortable for those in power.

India's constitutional commitment to freedom of speech cannot survive on assurances alone. It requires lawful orders, transparent procedures, independent scrutiny and effective remedies.

⚖️ THE LAW MUST NOT BECOME A SHORTCUT AROUND DUE PROCESS

The reporting distinguishes the takedown mechanism associated with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act from the separate blocking framework under Section 69A.

These are not interchangeable provisions. Their legal basis, procedures and safeguards matter. The public deserves clarity about which authority issued each order, what legal grounds were invoked and what opportunity affected users had to challenge it.

OUR DEMANDS

1. Publish regular, platform-wise statistics on government takedown orders, their legal grounds and their outcomes.
2. Ensure meaningful human and legal review of disputed or ambiguous directions.
3. Give affected users clear notice, subject to narrowly justified exceptions, and an effective appeal mechanism.
4. Disclose the safeguards governing automated integration between government portals and social-media platforms.
5. Ensure that peaceful dissent, journalism and legitimate political criticism are not suppressed through vague or overbroad directions.
6. Enable independent judicial scrutiny wherever legality or fundamental rights are contested.

India cannot call itself the world's largest democracy while treating transparency about restrictions on public speech as optional.

THE ISSUE IS NOT WHETHER GOVERNMENTS CAN ENFORCE THE LAW. THE ISSUE IS WHETHER THEY CAN DO SO WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY.

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful content—but it must also protect citizens' right to question the state.

When posts disappear, citizens deserve to know why. When orders are issued, the public deserves to know under what authority. And when lawful speech is wrongly removed, there must be a meaningful remedy.

Digital India must not become a system in which technology makes silencing citizens easier than answering them.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

A meticulously researched exposition in Digital Constitutionalism, Telecommunications Law, and Civil Liberties Jurisprudence by Rizmi Lia M. The article rigorously synthesises the evolving legal framework governing Internet Shutdowns, balancing National Security, Public Order, and Fundamental Rights within India's constitutional architecture.
  @the_hindu

UPSC Mains | Core Facts, Arguments & Insights:- 
Central Thesis: Internet Shutdowns are an extraordinary legal measure, permissible only under strict constitutional, statutory, and judicial safeguards, not as a routine administrative response.

Legal Framework: Internet suspension is governed by the Telecommunications Act, 2023 and the Telecommunications (Temporary Suspension of Services) Rules, 2024, replacing the Indian Telegraph Act, 1885 and 2017 Rules.

Permissible Grounds: Shutdowns are allowed only in cases of Public Emergency or Public Safety, supported by written reasons, competent authority approval, and defined objectives.

Doctrine of Proportionality: Authorities must adopt the Least Restrictive Measure; blanket internet suspension should be the last resort, not the first response.

Supreme Court Doctrine: In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020), the Supreme Court held that internet access is intrinsically linked to Article 19(1)(a) (Freedom of Speech & Expression) and Article 19(1)(g) (Freedom of Trade & Profession).

Judicial Safeguards: Every shutdown order must be Reasoned, Time-Bound, Published, Subject to Review, and Open to Judicial Scrutiny; Indefinite Shutdowns are Unconstitutional.

Implementation Concern: Despite the new legal regime, some States reportedly continue relying on outdated legal provisions, raising concerns over procedural compliance and rule of law.

Global Position: India continues to record one of the world's highest numbers of internet shutdowns, making digital governance and rights protection key policy concerns.

Democratic Impact: Internet shutdowns affect Freedom of Expression, Digital Economy, Education, Emergency Services, Business Continuity, and Citizen Access to Information.

Policy Imperative: Strengthen Legal Accountability, Transparent Decision-Making, Periodic Review, Targeted Restrictions, and Digital Rights Protection while preserving Public Order.

Author's Core Argument

> Internet shutdowns must remain an exceptional, legally proportionate, and judicially reviewable instrument. Democratic governance requires balancing legitimate security concerns with constitutional freedoms, ensuring that digital rights are not curtailed through excessive executive discretion.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
Since this story started trending, I have seen different versions of what happened...

Some people say the couple had s€xual intercourse inside a mosque in Makkah...Others say they only kissed... Some have even shared pictures claiming to show their execution.

I had to go search because online rumours sometimes are worris0me.

So, what exactly happened?

On Wednesday, 14 October 2026, Saudi Arabia announced the execution of two Bangladeshi nationals, a man and a woman, in the Makkah region.

According to Saudi Arabia's Ministry of Interior, the two had been arrested following an investigation and taken through legal proceedings... The court found them guilty of what the authorities described as an “immoral act” inside a mosque.

The court sentenced them to death under ta'zir, a category of discretionary punishment under Islamic law...

 According to the Saudi statement, the severity of the offence and the violation of the sanctity of the time and place were considered...The verdict was upheld and a royal order was issued for the executions.

But here is where the story becomes more complicated.

What exactly did the couple do inside the mosque?

The Saudi authorities did not publicly explain the precise act in their announcement... They did not identify the mosque or provide detailed information about the circumstances of the incident.

This is why different versions began circulating online, with some people claiming that the couple had s€x while others said they had only kissed.

However, subsequent reporting by The Daily Star in Bangladesh stated that a message from the Bangladesh mission's Labour Welfare Wing described the allegation as adultery inside a mosque.

So, while adultery was reported as the allegation, the full details of the incident have not been made public in the reports available.

And what did Bangladesh say?

Bangladesh said its diplomatic mission had not been informed before the executions took place.

After learning of the matter, the Bangladesh Consulate in Jeddah sought clarification from Saudi authorities. 

On 18 October, Bangladesh's Ministry of Foreign Affairs also sought an explanation from the Saudi ambassador.

By 19 October, Bangladesh was still seeking further information about the case.

Another report revealed that the two individuals' names had appeared on a list of prisoners previously shared with the Bangladeshi mission, but the list did not disclose that they had received death sentences.

A picture/video being shared as footage of this particular execution was fact-checked and found to be from an unrelated incident in 2015. 

It was not footage of the two Bangladeshis executed in October 2026.

This is another reminder that a video can be real while the story attached to it is false.

That is what I found....

Now, I am sharing this not to judge the couple, condemn Saudi Arabia, defend anybody or encourage anyone to disrespect the sanctity of a mosque.

I simply want us to separate what has been confirmed from what people are assuming.

We know that the executions were announced. 

We know what the Saudi authorities said about the conviction... We know that Bangladesh sought an explanation after learning of the executions.

But the precise details of what happened inside that mosque have not been fully established in the public reports available to anyone...

As Muslims, we can recognise the sanctity of the holy places while also being careful about what we say concerning people's lives, deaths and legal cases.

We do not have to invent details to make a story powerful... We do not have to take sides before understanding the facts.

Sometimes, the most responsible thing to say is simply, This is what we know, this is what has been reported and this is what we still do not know... 

People can talk down on your religion without any tangible/reasonable fact- check... Let them... It doesn't start today, so it won't end now...

©️Nafisah Usamot O
The MFE Talkspace...

text:
MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

text:
मोदी जी द्वारा दिए गए कल डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने झूठे विचार रखे जिनकी पोल खुल चुकी है।
दिल्ली में पत्रकारों, यू ट्यूबर,सोशल मीडिया एक्टिविस्ट को पीटा गिरफ्तार किया गया, सोशल मीडिया एकाउंट बंद किए जा रहे है लगातार।

कंपनियां हर महीने भारत सरकार को अपनी 'मासिक अनुपालन रिपोर्ट' (Monthly Compliance Report) सौंपती हैं
Facebook और Instagram (Meta): मेटा ने भारत के अन्दर 6 महीनों में 1.6 लाख (160,000) से अधिक अकाउंट्स पर सीधे बड़ी कार्रवाई की है।
• ट्विटर (X एक्स: एक महीने की अवधि में ही भारत में 5 लाख से अधिक अकाउंट्स को पूरी तरह बैन किया है। जिनमें कुछ समाचार पोर्टल और पत्रकारों के हैंडल भी शामिल थे।

गृह मंत्रालय के 'सहयोग पोर्टल' (Sahyog Portal) और IT एक्ट की धाराओं के तहत मार्च से जुलाई 2026 के बीच करीब 1.95 लाख (195,000) कंटेंट ब्लॉकिंग और टेकडाउन आदेश जारी किए गए। यह औसतन हर 68 सेकंड में एक आदेश के बराबर है।
• Instagram: सबसे ज़्यादा लगभग 1 लाख (100,000) ब्लॉकिंग आदेश मिले।
• Facebook: करीब 80,000 टेकडाउन और ब्लॉकिंग निर्देश दिए गए。
• YouTube: लगभग 15,000 आदेश जारी किए गए।

प्रधानमंत्री नरेंद्र मोदी ने नई दिल्ली में आयोजित आठवें ब्लूमबर्ग न्यू इकोनॉमी फोरम (Bloomberg New Economy Forum) में देश के डिजिटल मंचों और लोकतंत्र को लेकर अपने विचार रखे।
उन्होंने भारत को 'लोकतंत्र की जननी' (Mother of Democracy) बताया और कहा कि भारत में 100 से अधिक भाषाएं, करीब 80,000 पंजीकृत समाचार पत्र और 1,000 से ज्यादा सैटेलाइट टीवी चैनल मौजूद हैं।
उन्होंने बताया कि भारत में 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग यूट्यूब और 50 करोड़ से अधिक लोग इंस्टाग्राम का इस्तेमाल करते हैं, जो ऑनलाइन नागरिक चर्चाओं में सक्रिय रूप से भाग लेते हैं।
उन्होंने कहा कि इन डिजिटल मंचों ने एक ऐसा मंच तैयार किया है जहां नागरिक खुले तौर पर विचारों का आदान-प्रदान और राष्ट्रीय मुद्दों पर बहस करते हैं।

text:
A Hyderabad founder spent four months building a B2B SaaS product. CRM integrations, three pricing tiers, onboarding that actually worked.

Two weeks before launch his co-founder asked what the cookie banner said.

There was no cookie banner. There were two documents, and neither of them had been written for this product.

The Terms of Service came from a competitor’s site. The Privacy Policy came from a template generator. Both had been pasted in during week one and never opened again.

He reached out to us with fourteen days on the clock. He was not asking for a document set. He wanted to know whether what he already had would survive contact with a paying customer.

So we read both documents against the product, not against each other.

The Privacy Policy said the platform collects name, email, and company name. That was true as far as it went.

It said nothing about the session replay tool running on every page, recording mouse movement and clicks from every visitor. 

Nothing about the analytics platform receiving behaviour data on export. 

Nothing about the CRM integration pulling contact records out of the customer’s own account.

Three tools were processing user data and a user reading the policy would never know they existed.

Under the DPDP Act, 2023 and the Rules notified on 13 November 2025, the notice has to itemize what is collected, the purpose, the retention, and who it is shared with. 

A policy that names three fields and omits three processors is not a short policy. It is an inaccurate one.

Then the liability cap. The template had a blank where the number goes and nobody had filled it in, so the contract capped his liability at zero.

Founders hear that and assume it is maximum protection. It is the opposite. 

A limitation clause that strips out all liability is the one most likely to be read against the drafter, and under UK law an unreasonable exclusion can be struck down entirely, which leaves the liability uncapped. 

The clause meant to protect him was the one most likely to disappear in a dispute.

The acceptable use clause prohibited uploading anything illegal. It said nothing about who owns uploaded data, whether the platform could use it to improve the product, or what happens to it when a subscription ends.

This is B2B. Every upload was a business customer’s data, which usually means it was someone else’s customer data two steps down the chain. Silence in the Terms is not a neutral position on that. If anything in the stack learns from customer data, silence means it is happening without a license.

The part I keep seeing is the sequence. 

Founders treat legal documents as a launch-day chore, something to generate the night before, when they are actually a product specification written in another language. 

The documents describe what the software does. If nobody checks them against what the software does, they describe a different product.

What I found harder to watch here was how well everything else had been built. 

Four months of careful work, and the one artefact he had outsourced to a template site was the first thing an enterprise buyer would open.

Here is what we did in the fourteen days.

We mapped every tool with access to user data, including the ones installed by his developer and never documented anywhere.

We rewrote the privacy notice to cover all of them, with purpose, retention, and third-party sharing set out against each.

We put a defensible number in the liability cap and rebuilt the clause around it.

We drafted the data ownership, permitted use, and model training position, plus deletion and export on termination.

We added the IT Rules disclosures, legal entity details and a named grievance officer, to the footer and the Terms.

The product launched three weeks later with a complete set. One week after that, the first enterprise prospect asked for a security and compliance review before signing. He had answers.

The comparison is not close. Two weeks of drafting before launch, against a DPDP penalty regime that runs up to ₹250 crore for security safeguard failures, and against the thing that actually kills early deals, which is a procurement team deciding you are too much work to onboard.

So here are three things to check before your next customer invite goes out.

Open your Privacy Policy and list every tool on your site that touches user data. Analytics, session replay, chat widget, CRM, email platform. If an SDK is installed and not named, your notice is wrong. Naming the obvious ones and skipping the rest is not a shorter policy.

Find the number in your liability cap. If the clause is blank, inherited, or set to zero, that is not conservative drafting. It is the clause your buyer’s counsel will spend the most time on.

Read what your Terms say about uploaded data. Ownership, permitted use, what happens on termination, and whether anything in your stack improves on it. If the document is silent on all four, you are relying on an assumption you never wrote down.

Two dates are now fixed. The Consent Manager framework switches on 13 November 2026. The obligations on notice, consent, security, and data principal rights apply from 13 May 2027.

Most founders who send us their documents believe the legal side is handled because the pages exist. 

The pages existing and the pages matching the product are different things, and the buyer’s counsel is the one who checks.

text:
Meta must stop silently withholding the Instagram accounts of independent journalists in India

13 October 2026

Since 9 October 2026, Instagram has made the accounts of several independent journalists covering the protests in Delhi unavailable in India. Utkarsh Gaur’s main account was withheld on 9 October, and Sunny Tomar’s soon after. On the night of 12 October, Instagram withheld the account of Shubhangi Das Gupta, a 22-year-old independent journalist, and her secondary account now appears to face the same action. Today, Journo Mirror’s account was withheld in India. Each received the same notice, that Instagram had, “temporarily restricted access to this account pursuant to legal requirements under India’s Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules.” The notice does not say which authority made the demand, which rule was invoked, which post was objected to, or when the “temporary” restriction ends. It arrives as a no-reply notification after the account has gone dark, with no prior warning and no reason.

The same day, IANS and ANI, citing Delhi Police sources, reported that around 500 posts “spreading rumours or trying to create unrest among people” had been taken down. On 12 October, PTI had put the figure at 300, which means about 200 more in one day. The police have not said which posts were removed, from which platforms, under which provision, or whether anyone who posted them was told. We are also receiving reports of WhatsApp accounts being shut down and of mobile numbers being put through fresh KYC verification that leaves them unusable while it is pending. All of this comes alongside a timeline in which there was suspension of internet services and public transport in the heart of the national capital.

IFF condemns Meta’s withholding of entire journalist accounts on the strength of an unnamed “legal requirement”, and the Delhi Police’s practice of announcing a running censorship tally through anonymous sources. Meta must restore these accounts, tell every affected user who asked for the restriction and under what law, and stop turning demands about particular posts into the silencing of entire accounts.
The IT Rules, 2021, on which Meta’s notice relies, give it two routes to restrict content. The notice meets the conditions of neither. If Meta acted on a government demand, the route is Rule 3(1)(d). If Meta acted on its own, Rule 4(8) requires it, as a significant social media intermediary, to notify the user before disabling access, explain the grounds, and give an adequate opportunity to dispute the action. None of this happened. In this situation at present the entire burden will be shifted to the user to seek remedy under Rules 3(2) and 3A, where a user must first go to Meta’s Grievance Officer, who has 15 days, and then to the Grievance Appellate Committee, which has 30 more. In our experience these timelines are often not met, and a grievance against unnamed “legal requirements” is likely to be answered by pointing back to them. Whatever the intention, the effect is to keep a journalist off the platform for more than six weeks, exactly when her reporting matters most.

The Delhi Police figures raise their own questions. “Rumour” is not a ground for restricting speech under Article 19(2).  A count of 500 posts announced through unnamed sources does not let anyone tell whether a post was fabricated or simply showed something the police did not want seen. Nor is it obvious that 200 reasoned intimations, each signed by an officer of DIG rank and each identifying the provision, the unlawful act and the exact URL, were issued in a single day.

Our demands

1) Meta should restore every account withheld in connection with the protests where the underlying demand, if any, concerned specific posts, and restrict no more than the URLs named in a lawful reasoned intimation.
2) Meta should tell each affected user in writing which authority made the demand, the issuing officer’s rank, the provision relied on, the content identified, and when the restriction will end.
3) Meta should disclose whether its systems automatically extend demands about individual posts to entire accounts, and stop any such escalation immediately.
4) The Delhi Police should publish the takedown requests it has issued, with their number, platforms, provisions, issuing officers and reasons, as Anuradha Bhasin requires.
5) MeitY should ensure notice and a hearing to every person whose content is restricted, publish the outcome of the monthly Secretary-level review under Rule 3(1)(d), and stop using Section 79(3)(b), the Sahyog Portal and “temporary” restrictions under the IT Rules to bypass the safeguards of Section 69A.
If you have been affected

**SOCIAL MEDIA CENSORSHIP CANNOT OPERATE IN SECRECY — CITIZENS HAVE A RIGHT TO KNOW WHY THEIR CONTENT IS BLOCKED**

**PUNJAB & HARYANA HIGH COURT REAFFIRMS NATURAL JUSTICE AND DIGITAL FREEDOM**

In an important development for freedom of expression and digital rights, the Punjab and Haryana High Court has reportedly held that social media users whose content is targeted for blocking must receive a copy of the government's intimation sent to the intermediary, immediately after it is issued.

This is a significant affirmation of a fundamental democratic principle: **The government cannot exercise censorship powers without procedural fairness and accountability.**

**WHY THIS MATTERS FOR DEMOCRACY**

Article 19(1)(a) of the Indian Constitution guarantees freedom of speech and expression, subject to constitutionally permissible restrictions under Article 19(2).

When the government seeks to block a citizen's social media content, that citizen should have a meaningful opportunity to understand the grounds for the action and pursue an appropriate legal remedy.

The principles of natural justice demand transparency, fairness and protection against arbitrary executive action.

**FIVE QUESTIONS EVERY CITIZEN SHOULD ASK**

1. Why should a citizen discover that their content has been blocked without knowing the government's reasons?

2. How can someone challenge censorship if the government withholds the communication underlying the blocking action?

3. Should social media intermediaries be allowed to implement government blocking directions without adequate procedural safeguards for affected users?

4. Who ensures that blocking powers are not misused to suppress criticism, dissent or legitimate political opposition?

5. If government action is lawful and justified, why should procedural transparency be feared?

**NATIONAL SECURITY CANNOT BECOME A BLANKET EXCUSE FOR ARBITRARY CENSORSHIP.**

Legitimate restrictions may sometimes be necessary under the Constitution. But every restriction must satisfy applicable legal requirements, and safeguards must prevent disproportionate interference with fundamental rights.

This reported ruling is particularly relevant to independent journalists, activists, opposition voices, whistleblowers and ordinary citizens who rely on social media to participate in democratic debate.

**OUR DEMAND**

Every government-initiated content-blocking process must respect constitutional protections, applicable disclosure requirements, due process and meaningful access to judicial review.

The right to criticise the government is not a favour granted by those in power. It is an essential part of constitutional democracy.

**A DEMOCRACY THAT SILENCES QUESTIONS WEAKENS ITSELF. A DEMOCRACY THAT PROTECTS DISSENT STRENGTHENS ITS CONSTITUTION.**
