Exemption from Liability of Intermediaries in Certain Cases

Section 79 of the Information Technology Act, 2000 provides legal protection to intermediaries against liability for third-party content hosted or transmitted through their platforms.

An intermediary includes social media platforms, internet service providers, web-hosting companies, search engines, and similar online service providers. Examples include X (Twitter), Facebook, and YouTube.

Sub-section (1)

An intermediary shall not be liable for any third-party information, data, or communication link made available or hosted by it, subject to the conditions specified in the Act.

Sub-section (2)

This protection applies only if:

The intermediary's role is limited to providing access to a communication system through which information is transmitted, temporarily stored, or hosted;

The intermediary does not initiate the transmission;

The intermediary does not select the receiver of the transmission;

The intermediary does not select or modify the information contained in the transmission; and

The intermediary observes due diligence and complies with the requirements prescribed under the Act and the applicable rules.

Sub-section (3)

The protection under Section 79 shall not apply if:

1. The intermediary has conspired, abetted, aided, or induced the commission of an unlawful act; or

2. Upon receiving actual knowledge, or upon being notified by the appropriate Government or its agency that any information, data, or communication link hosted on its computer resource is being used to commit an unlawful act, the intermediary fails to expeditiously remove or disable access to such material while preserving evidence.

Explanation

The term “Third Party Information” refers to any information dealt with by an intermediary in its capacity as an intermediary.

Practical Significance

Section 79 provides a “safe Harbour” to intermediaries. As a result, social media platforms and other intermediaries are generally not automatically liable for content posted by their users. However, if they participate in unlawful activities or fail to act after receiving a valid legal notice or government direction, they may lose the protection granted under Section 79.

The scope of this provision was further clarified by the Supreme Court of India in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India. The Court held that “Actual knowledge” for the purposes of Section 79 generally arises through a court order or a notification issued by a competent government authority, requiring the intermediary to take appropriate action.

text:
$QCOM v $ARM

We had closing arguments in the bench trial today.

Judge Noreika spent three and a half hours grilling both sides, cutting right through polished lawyer arguments to demand cold hard facts. 

To remind folks the bench trial covers the equitable issues the jury did not decide. Those include Qualcomm's California Unfair Competition Law (UCL) claims alleging input foreclosure and anticompetitive conduct, and Qualcomm's contract claim that Arm breached Section 14.1.B of the 2013 ALA by failing to negotiate a v10 architecture license in good faith. 

The General stepped up to the podium and went straight on the attack. She framed Arm's entire conduct around an internal meeting from December 2021 where Rene Haas pitched SoftBank on taking Arm vertical to build its own chips so that the rest of the industry, including Qualcomm, would be hosed. 

She immediately went in on Haas's credibility. She reminded the Court that during the December 2024 trial in this very courtroom, Haas testified under oath that Arm does not build chips and Arm does not sell chips. Yet internal evidence now proves that at that exact moment, hundreds of Arm engineers were designing physical silicon and Arm had already signed a Statement of Work with Meta. She argued Haas deliberately concealed Arm's vertical plans to entrench its position before anyone could object.

She walked through the Samsung evidence from October 2022, where Masayoshi Son and Haas flew to Korea right after suing Qualcomm, falsely telling Samsung leadership that Qualcomm's license expired in 2024 and that Qualcomm would be unable to supply Snapdragon processors for 2025 Galaxy phones. She argued this was a calculated roadmap to clear the board and replace Qualcomm with Arm's own custom silicon.

Then Judge Noreika jumped in with her first major reality check. 

Right out of the gate, Judge Noreika warned Dunn to abandon the UCL consumer test and focus entirely on the competitor test, signaling she is highly skeptical that consumer balancing applies. 

When Dunn laid out what Qualcomm is asking for in its proposed injunction, a court ordered v10 license, an extension of the ALA term, v10 financial rates benchmarked against Apple and Nvidia, immediate delivery of all v10 specs, and an order enjoining Arm from disadvantaging ALA licensees, Judge Noreika pushed back quite hard.

Paraphrased based on my memory: "I don't know what that means. If that is what you really want me to order, that sounds like me having to run these companies. And trust me  nobody wants that. You want them to give you your old deal, they say no, you say that is contempt, and I have to play your moms."

Judge Noreika was equally blunt about Qualcomm's antitrust theories. She openly questioned why Qualcomm was citing federal monopolization cases like Kodak and Aspen Skiing under a California state statute without ever bringing a federal Sherman Act claim or defining a relevant antitrust market. 

Dunn pushed back, arguing that under California's Cel Tech decision, a plaintiff only has to show a significant threat to competition, not a completed monopoly. She argued that Microsoft and Google have no incentive to build custom cores under their restrictive deals, leaving Apple in its closed garden and Nvidia in a cozy relationship, meaning Qualcomm is the only independent merchant core designer left.

On v10, Dunn showed again the internal emails from 2020 where Arm account lead Lynn Couillard called Qualcomm's v10 election clever and admitted she saw no reason why it could not hold. She contrasted that with Arm licensing executive Lapinski emailing about delaying negotiations later in bad faith. Judge Noreika remarked that Lapinski's email read like British humor, but Dunn retorted that it was not funny when Arm actually carried out the delay for four years.

Dunn highlighted the July 2025 CEO meeting where Amon sat at a whiteboard offering MFN plus 5 percent, plus 10 percent, or whatever premium Arm needed to let Qualcomm compete, while Haas brushed it off as hypothetical. She pointed out that Arm's formal counteroffer demanded a 15x increase in mobile royalties, totaling more in royalties for mobile CPUs alone than all licensees paid Arm across all products last year. 

Dunn ended by citing recent tech injunctions like Epic v. Apple and Google search, arguing that without v10 specifications Qualcomm cannot design future silicon, creating catastrophic irreparable harm before reserving the rest of her time.

LoCascio took the podium for Arm to tackle the v10 contract claims under Section 14.1.B of the ALA. 

He started by shooting down Dunn's claim that Qualcomm still lacks ACK patches, telling the Court that quarterly test updates containing all bug fixes were delivered continuously and that Qualcomm never filed another complaint after the jury verdict.

LoCascio argued that the entire dispute boils down to Qualcomm trying to block Arm from competing in data centers. He hammered Qualcomm's biggest evidentiary vulnerability. That Qualcomm claims Arm's proposed rates are existential and prevent it from competing, but Qualcomm never put on any evidence of its chip selling prices, its gross margins, or how the proposed rates actually impact its bottom line. 

On the contract language, LoCascio argued that Section 14.1.B.1 required mutual agreement on future technology terms at the midpoint. He argued that in May 2020 Qualcomm asked for an amendment, was told v10 was not being developed, and then went completely silent for five years without making a formal offer until 2025. He showed that Google and Microsoft did not add v10 in 2020 either, they negotiated and added v10 in 2025. 

On good faith, LoCascio argued that an agreement to negotiate does not mean Arm must offer terms Qualcomm likes. Section 14.1.B does not contain an MFN clause, a FRAND commitment, or a percentage cap. Arm is legally entitled to seek market value for its IP.

He then took direct aim at Qualcomm's MFN plus 5 percent proposal, branding it a mix and match menu card. He argued Qualcomm wanted to cherry pick the best parts of everyone else's agreements, taking a startup low upfront fee like Nuvia, taking Apple's low rate in mobile, and taking Nvidia's rate in data centers.

LoCascio then defended Arm's proposed v10 rates, putting up slides to argue the numbers are reasonable when you account for core counts and chip prices. 

In mobile, he argued phone chips in 2013 sold for a fraction of today's flagship processors. He leaked the price Qualcomm sells their chips at which are $220. He then argued Qualcomm's 2013 cap of $1.88 equaled roughly 23 cents per core on an eight core phone. He pointed to defense evidence, claiming Arm offered a Total Compute royalty that serves as a cap for consumer devices up to eight cores, arguing the uplift over v8 is completely in line with what Qualcomm agreed to pay when transitioning from v7 to v8.

In data center servers, LoCascio argued the 2013 cap of $1.88 was designed for low power mobile chips and never contemplated massive 128 core or 288 core server processors selling for thousands of dollars. He argued Arm's proposed non consumer per core rate represents a fair percentage of selling price for chips packing hundreds of cores.

Before LoCascio sat down, Judge Noreika hit him with a sharp question on Haas's credibility. She brought up Haas testifying in 2024 that Arm does not build or sell chips when Arm engineers were already working on silicon.

LoCascio scrambled, arguing Haas was referring to an earlier, unrelated internal chip project that was shuttered rather than the current data center effort. But Judge Noreika was visibly unconvinced, noting that Haas's statement was completely general and did not specify any particular chip.

Jason Wilcox for Arm took over to address the legal standards under California's UCL and why Qualcomm is barred from injunctive relief.

Wilcox started with the jury's verdict on tortious interference regarding the Meta letter and Bloomberg leak. He argued that under Third Circuit law and California equity, those events happened two years ago in 2022 and 2024. Qualcomm already pursued its legal remedy, and the jury awarded what it deemed appropriate ($1 nominal damages). Because the UCL provides strictly prospective injunctive relief, past conduct cannot justify an injunction.

Wilcox then worked to attack Qualcomm's input foreclosure claim. He reminded the Court that under her Daubert ruling, Professor Posner was barred from calling Arm a monopolist because Posner never defined an antitrust market. Posner admitted on cross examination that he performed no quantitative economic modeling on foreclosure risk and admitted he could only speculate on whether Microsoft and Google were cowed by Arm.

Wilcox highlighted another defense evidence, which contains 20 pages of public statements from companies like Broadcom, Marvell, Samsung, and MediaTek praising Arm's entry into data center chips. He argued Arm entered the market because customers like Meta needed energy efficient silicon that existing vendors were not supplying, making Arm's entry procompetitive.

On antitrust law, Wilcox cited Supreme Court precedent in Colgate, Trinko, and Pacific Bell, as well as Judge Gorsuch's Tenth Circuit opinion in Novell v. Microsoft, establishing that a firm has no antitrust duty to deal and has the right to choose its licensees and protect its IP (Which I thought was a stupid cite I can go into why if anyone cares in a reply) He then cited Beverage v. Apple, which confirmed that California's UCL cannot override the Colgate doctrine to force a company to license on terms it opposes.

Then came the biggest moment for Arm. When Wilcox began arguing that Arm's past letters and deliverable withholding posed no ongoing risk, Judge Noreika interrupted him and gave Arm a concession:

Paraphrased (Judge Noreika):
"I believe you, there is no threat of future violations. What's next?"

Wilcox wrapped up by emphasizing that specific performance and judicial rate setting require continuous judicial supervision, which federal courts have rejected since the 1970s.

With both sides done with their prepared remarks, Judge Noreika called Dunn and LoCascio back for a round of questioning.

Judge Noreika questioned Dunn on the lack of proof that Arm was sacrificing short term profits under Aspen Skiing, and pressed her on why the Court should ignore public statements from major tech companies praising Arm's chip entry. 

She then pressed Dunn hard on the menu card issue, was Qualcomm really demanding MFN plus 5 percent across separate product silos? 

Dunn clarified that Qualcomm is in all product segments, whereas Apple is only in mobile and Nvidia is in data centers. She explained that Qualcomm was forced to propose segment benchmarking because Qualcomm was flying blind, Apple's rates were shielded by a protective order and Nvidia's license was never produced, while Arm rejected every single benchmark structure Qualcomm put forward.

Judge Noreika then hit Dunn with what I take as core evidentiary flaw in Qualcomm's case. She asked (paraphrased): "Where is the evidence that you can't compete? For all I know, on 2013 rates Qualcomm's profit margin was 99.98%, now with the rates going up margins would be 75 percent. Where is the evidence that you can't compete?"

Dunn explained that Qualcomm cannot compete because in mobile, Arm's offer contains no cap at all, resulting in proposed rates that are 34.5x higher in the second period and can exceed the entire selling price of the device. 

Dunn pointed directly to the Total Compute smartphone cap that LoCascio had bragged about earlier. She cited defnese evidence and Dr. Kennedy's testimony, exposing that Arm's proposed cap strictly excludes any processor that includes an integrated modem. 

Because virtually every single Snapdragon mobile processor Qualcomm manufactures incorporates an integrated modem, Arm's supposed cap is completely illusory for Qualcomm's actual business.

Judge Noreika called LoCascio back to the podium and told him she wanted to hear about nothing else oter than did Arm's proposed smartphone cap exclude chips with a modem?

He was forced to concede on the record that the cap distinguishes between standalone processors and chips with an integrated cellular modem, attempting to argue that Apple buys modems separately. 

Judge Noreika was either unimpressed or confused by LoCascio's aswer and told LoCascio that he had to explain that further in his post trial filings. 

Dunn seized the opening on rebuttal, reminding the Court that Qualcomm is not asking the Judge to set dollar rates, but rather to find that Arm's bad faith conduct and unworkable carveouts violated the contract and the UCL.

Before adjourning, LoCascio asked if post trial briefing on the jury verdict could be paused until Judge Noreika issues her ruling on the September Section 8.3 bench trial. 

LoCascio noted that Judge Noreika previously stated at the pretrial conference that she was 98 percent inclined to strike down Section 8.3 as an illegal liquidated damages penalty. If she confirms that ruling, Arm will not need to move for a new trial on liability. 

Judge Noreika refused to delay the post trial schedule, telling Arm to preserve the issue with a conditional motion in the 2 percent chance she changes her mind. 

The Court set a briefing schedule of 50 pages for opening post trial briefs and findings of fact, with 25 pages for replies.

So where does this leave us?

On the big money remedies, Arm is clearly in the driver's seat. Section 8.3 is 98 percent dead, meaning Arm dodges the $4 billion royalty holiday. 

On the UCL, Qualcomm seems to be running uphill against a brick wall. Judge Noreika's statement that "I believe you, there is no threat of future violations" practically shuts the door on a broad forward looking injunction against Arm's business practices, and her flat refusal to "play your moms" means she will never order a vague decree telling Arm not to disadvantage Qualcomm. 

A lot of folks will ask wait, didn't the jury already find Arm liable for a UCL violation regarding Meta under both the competitor and consumer tests? How can the Judge toss Qualcomm's UCL claims?

Under the Seventh Amendment, Judge Noreika is legally bound by the jury's finding that Arm's 2024 cancellation letter to Meta and the Bloomberg leak were unfair business acts. But the jury already gave Qualcomm its legal remedy for that past conduct(one dollar in nominal damages). 

Under California equity, an injunction cannot be used to punish past conduct. An injunction can only issue to stop threatened, ongoing future harm. Because Arm retracted the termination threat two years ago and has not sent letters since, Judge Noreika agreed with Arm that there is no threat of future violations. 

Qualcomm tried to use the jury's Meta verdict as a launchpad to demand sweeping structural relief under the UCL, like barring Arm from disadvantaging ALA licensees. Judge Noreika rejected that leap, refusing to use a past customer letter as an excuse to play the FTC and regulate Arm's business model. 

The v10 fight is different because it is primarily a contract claim under Count 9. That is where Arm is actually on defense. Judge Noreika knows Haas misled the court in 2024 about building chips, knows Arm sat on Qualcomm's election for four years, and caught LoCascio red handed trying to pass off a smartphone cap that excludes modem chips. 

The most realistic outcome. Judge Noreika rules Section 8.3 is an unenforceable penalty, tosses Qualcomm's broad UCL structural claims, but rules that Qualcomm timely elected under Section 14.1.B and orders Arm back to the table to negotiate in good faith without the modem exclusion gimmicks, while refusing to act as a rate setter herself. 

We will see how both teams package their 50 page briefs over the coming weeks, but today proved once again that in Judge Noreika's courtroom, rhetoric without cold hard balance sheet evidence will get you nowhere.

How I ($1MM/year seller) find winning Amazon FBA products in 2026

Quick context: ~9 years selling on Amazon, 3 brands, ~1,500 SKUs (mostly toys & games), 3 VAs, $1MM/year at ~40% margin. Numbers verified by https://t.co/HnGPqhlwMu and the mods of r/FulfillmentByAmazon: https://t.co/e14qmNmwm5

Below is the process my team and I use to find products. I've broken down a bunch of Amazon stores over the last few months, and the same process keeps working for me, so here it is. No tool needed to start, just Amazon and a spreadsheet.

STEP 1 - Start from stores that already win, not from keywords or individual products

• Keyword tools tell you what people search for. They don't tell you who makes money.
• Individual products also don't tell the whole story - I have 1,500 SKUs, most of them don't make much money, but combined they made me a business.
• Find brands that started recently (6-12 months) and already sell well - that proves the niche is still open to new entrants
• Amazon's own "X+ bought in past month" on each listing, summed across their ASINs, gives you a revenue estimate that's surprisingly close

STEP 2 - Ask ONE question: where did the founder add value ?

• Almost everything on Amazon is made by the same Chinese factories. If the only thing you add is a logo, you're competing on price - and that's a race to zero margin
• The products I keep seeing with HIGH margins are ones where the customer pays for something made once and sold many times: a DESIGN (puzzles, card games, kitchen gadgets with a cute/creative shape), or a product paired with an app/course
• People buy a puzzle for the picture, not the cardboard. That's why a $3 puzzle sells for $20 - same goes for card games, posters, or anything like that
• This is my framework from running my own brand, not something I can prove - but the stores I analyse fit it a lot
• I stay away from food and supplements - no experience there, so I won't pretend to advise on them (but they do essentially follow the same pattern - create a good recipe once and sell the food many times)

STEP 3 - Work out the real margin (this kills 80% of ideas)

Per-unit economics for the store you're looking at:

• Revenue = "bought in past month" x price, for every ASIN
• COGS = ask 3-5 suppliers on Alibaba for a quote on the same product at 100 MOQ. Real quotes, not guesses
• FBA fees + 15% referral fee - Amazon's revenue calculator does this
• PPC = CPC x monthly search volume x estimated CTR, for the keywords they bid on
• What's left is profit. I mostly ignore anything that ends up under ~25% margin

STEP 4 - Check how they get their sales

• Almost no PPC and still selling? The product itself converts. Great sign.
• Bringing traffic from outside of Amazon ? You'll have to understand if you can replicate their methods
• Sales spread across many SKUs, or one hero SKU ? One hero SKU = you have to win one fight. Many SKUs = they have a design pipeline you'd have to match

STEP 5 - Price the validation, not the dream

• Estimate how much it would cost you to test each brand you're thinking of launching. At the end of the day, in order to succeed, you'll need multiple tries (nobody has a 100% success rate). You want to try as many businesses as possible, as quickly as possible, for as cheap as possible.
• Cost to test = MOQ (e.g. 100 units x $5.40 = $540) + shipping + ONE month of ads on a few long tail keywords
• Some products you might be able to POD (print on demand) - that is, only *produce* the product AFTER you get the order. This is NOT dropshipping. You might even have to do it at a loss per order. This is just to validate demand. If you see there is demand for your product - shut off the listing and go produce it in China.
• If you can't test it for well under your budget, it's not a validation, it's a bet

WHY AM I GIVING THIS AWAY ?

• Fair question - I'd ask it too
• I used to think I should keep the good niches "secret". I don't anymore - people who know how to research will find them either way, and there's still a LOT of work and risk to take before any niche pays you.
• There's a huge amount of good niches to get into, but an even huger amount of niches that will DEFINITELY lose you money.
• I see Amazon newbies making the most basic mistakes all the time - because they don't understand that they gotta ADD VALUE to make money.
• What do I get out of it ? Nothing right now. Go check for yourself - the website and the case studies are completely free. You will see why the products there make money - they are good products where the founder added value to their customers' lives.
• The site is free to browse, no paywall

All the case studies are on my website, https://t.co/UvYlJ6HVeE (disclosure: I built it). It's more in depth than my posts - suppliers, keywords they rank/advertise on, graphs, etc.

India's voter rolls run on a platform where a State's access can be switched off and on from the centre. That's what an audit of Election Commission's own portal has found.
As reported by @sreeparna_c in @the_hindu , an audit of ECINET by the civic-tech initiative @Charchagram_ authored by data scientist Saurav Rajput, an alumnus of IIT Delhi and IIM Calcutta, has found the following.

🔹A State by State switch for voters forms. The code carries a message: View enumeration form details is not enabled for selected State. Access to voters enumeration forms can be turned on or off one State at a time.
🔹A disable button for every State Nodal Officer. ECINET has a State Nodal Officer management area with a built in disable action. Each SNO row has a disable button & the pop up reads: On disabling this State Nodal Officer, the user will no longer be able to access the application.
In Rajput's words: This seems a full account level block. The text doesn't describe a partial restriction or a role downgrade.
🔹A Bengal only lock. The audit has also found a feature that can bar EROs & AEROs only in West Bengal from reviewing voters enumeration forms and viewing the notice & hearing dashboard.
🔹Official only code that anyone can read. ECINET's login page loads a large JavaScript file before anyone logs in. It contains labels, menu names, screen routes & API paths meant only for officials, and anyone can open it. Rajput said: Even some features which are sitting behind the login credentials are available in the front end code. For the database holding India's voter rolls, that is a serious security concern.

Now set this against what the Election Commission told the country.
On September 24, the ECI said ECINET is a decentralised platform & that nobody else can perform their statutory function on ECINet, including any other officer of ECI.

If a State's access to voters' forms can be switched off centrally & a State Nodal Officer can be locked out of the application completely, then ECINET is not the decentralised platform Commission described. It has a central switch.

This goes to the heart of the objections raised by 2 of the Commission's own members, Election Commissioners Sukhbir Singh Sandhu & Vivek Joshi, over the centralisation of ECINET and the electoral roll database.

Under the law, the EROs hold statutory authority over the electoral roll. A platform that can shut States out of their own voters data hands that power to whoever controls the switch.

Questions must be answered -
🔹Who has the power to switch off a State's access to enumeration forms, & who has the power to disable a State Nodal Officer?
🔹Has any State ever been switched off? If so, which State, when & for how long?
🔹Has any State Nodal Officer ever been disabled & on whose order?
🔹Why does ECINET's code contain a lock that applies only to West Bengal?
🔹Why is code meant only for officials publicly readable on the login page of India's voter database?
🔹How does the Commission reconcile all of this with its September 24 claim that ECINET is decentralised?

When a system can switch States off at will, the States are not in control of their own voter rolls. Whoever holds the switch is & our nation has a right to know whose hand is on it.
The voter roll belongs to the people of India, not to whoever controls the switch.

INDIA'S VOTING RIGHTS DEMAND TRANSPARENCY, NOT SUSPICION

Former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa has raised serious concerns about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. Speaking at a citizens’ convention on 13 October, he alleged that voters were being removed on suspicion about their citizenship rather than on the basis of sufficient evidence.

According to The Wire's report, Lavasa also alleged that Electoral Registration Officers (EROs)—the officials legally authorised to delete names—were denied access to the Election Commission's centrally controlled ECINET software. He questioned the legality and fairness of a system in which officials responsible for electoral rolls may not have effective access to the tools needed to discharge their statutory duties.

These are serious allegations from a former Election Commissioner. They demand a clear, evidence-based response from the Election Commission.

THE APPEALS FIGURES RAISE ANOTHER IMPORTANT QUESTION

According to figures from an Election Commission report submitted to the Supreme Court, approximately 38.3 lakh appeals relating to SIR in West Bengal were filed before tribunals:

- 22.2 lakh appeals concerned voters excluded from the rolls who sought relief.
- 16.1 lakh appeals challenged the inclusion of voters whose names had been retained or restored.

These figures do not, by themselves, prove that every deletion was wrongful or that the entire process was politically motivated. But they demonstrate the enormous scale of the dispute and the need for transparent, independently scrutinizable decisions.

When an eligible citizen's name is removed, the consequences are not merely administrative. That person may lose the practical ability to exercise the constitutional right to vote.

THE QUESTIONS THE ECI MUST ANSWER

1. Were all deletions supported by individualised evidence and the procedures required by law?
2. Did authorised Electoral Registration Officers retain the powers and system access necessary to make lawful decisions?
3. Why are so many cases being contested before appellate tribunals?
4. How many excluded voters have been restored, how many exclusions have been upheld, and on what grounds?
5. What effective safeguards ensure that poor people, migrants, elderly citizens and people lacking extensive documentation are not unfairly excluded?

The Election Commission must publish clear, verifiable, category-wise data and explain the safeguards used to prevent wrongful deletion.

THE PRINCIPLE IS SIMPLE: CLEAN ELECTORAL ROLLS MUST NOT COME AT THE COST OF ELIGIBLE VOTERS.

The objective of accurate voter lists is legitimate. Removing deceased persons and genuine duplicate entries matters. But suspicion, a database discrepancy or an administrative mismatch should not replace a fair procedure grounded in evidence and law.

Every eligible voter must have a meaningful opportunity to establish eligibility, challenge an erroneous deletion and obtain timely relief before an election.

Demanding answers from the Election Commission is not an attack on democracy. It is a demand that a constitutional institution fulfil its responsibility to protect the integrity of the electoral process—and every eligible citizen's right to participate in it.

NO WRONGFUL DELETION. NO ARBITRARY EXCLUSION. NO SELECTIVE ACCOUNTABILITY.

Let the evidence be examined impartially. Let the Commission answer legitimate questions transparently. Where violations are established, accountability must follow.

OUR DEMOCRACY MUST COUNT EVERY ELIGIBLE VOTER—NOT MAKE CITIZENS FIGHT FOR THE RIGHT TO BE COUNTED.

Credit: The Wire

Did anyone accuse the Election Commission of being biased or campaigning against the government? Did the government have to rush to its defence? Or was the Election Commission simply exercising its constitutional independence?

In 2013, following the Supreme Court’s intervention, VVPAT was introduced to strengthen transparency and build confidence among voters and political parties. The Supreme Court recognised that an independently verifiable paper trail was indispensable to free and fair elections.

Now look at what is happening.

When questions were raised about the extraordinary increase in reported voter turnout after 5 PM, political parties and citizens sought access to CCTV footage and election records.

The Punjab and Haryana High Court directed the Election Commission to provide the relevant footage and records. What followed?

Instead of making election records more accessible, the Central Government amended Rule 93 of the Conduct of Election Rules in December 2024, on the Election Commission’s recommendation, restricting public access to CCTV footage and other electronic election records.

Subsequently, the Election Commission introduced instructions permitting the destruction of CCTV footage and other recordings after just 45 days where no election petition had been filed.

Why should evidence relating to the conduct of elections be made inaccessible and then destroyed when transparency is precisely what establishes public confidence?

The Supreme Court rejected the demand for 100% VVPAT verification in 2024. But what is the purpose of an independently verifiable paper trail if its comprehensive verification is resisted? The very purpose of introducing VVPAT was to strengthen public confidence in election results.

And now we are witnessing something even more disturbing.

Instead of concentrating on enrolling every eligible citizen, the electoral roll revision has resulted in the removal of approximately 13 crore names. Genuine voters are being forced to struggle to establish their eligibility and recover their voting rights.

With an adult population exceeding 100 crore, the Election Commission must explain how many eligible citizens remain outside the electoral rolls and how many have been wrongly excluded.

The Election Commission’s constitutional responsibility is to ensure that every eligible citizen can vote, not to make citizens struggle to protect their existing voting rights.

Look at the complete reversal.

Earlier, the Election Commission encouraged citizens to vote, expanded participation and introduced measures to strengthen public confidence.

#ElectionCommissionOfIndia

WHEN A VOTER QUESTIONS THE SYSTEM, THE SYSTEM MUST ANSWER—NOT EXPECT CITIZENS TO LAUGH OFF THEIR FEARS.

“Gyanesh ji, is baar kiska vote delete kar rahe hain?”

In this video, the creator says she received a message that appeared to relate to Form 7, used for objections to names in the electoral roll. She checked the Election Commission portal and noticed a troubling mismatch: her name and reference number appeared, but a phone notification reportedly displayed another person's name, Kuldeep Singh.

IS THIS A TECHNICAL ERROR, A DATA MISMATCH OR SOMETHING MORE SERIOUS?

The video alone does not establish the cause, and it would be premature to accuse anyone of deliberate manipulation. But the discrepancy deserves a clear explanation from the Election Commission.

Every eligible voter has the right to expect accurate records, transparent procedures and a fair opportunity to challenge any wrongful deletion. No citizen should have to wonder whether their vote is at risk because of confusing notifications or unexplained discrepancies.

The Election Commission should clarify:

- Why did the notification reportedly show a different person's name?
- Was any Form 7 objection actually filed, and against whose electoral entry?
- What safeguards prevent wrongful objections or deletion of eligible voters?
- How can affected citizens verify their status and obtain timely correction?

A VOTER'S RIGHT IS NOT A JOKE. ELECTORAL TRANSPARENCY IS NOT OPTIONAL.

If it is a technical error, correct it and explain it. If there is evidence of misuse, investigate independently and hold those responsible accountable.

Democracy requires more than asking citizens to trust the process. It requires a process that earns their trust through accuracy, transparency and accountability.

EVERY ELIGIBLE VOTE MATTERS. EVERY DISCREPANCY DESERVES AN ANSWER.

FORMER ELECTION COMMISSIONER RAISES ALARM: IS THE SIR PROCESS PRIORITISING VOTER DELETION OVER VOTER INCLUSION?
https://t.co/CzerQNMRpL

INDIA'S VOTING RIGHTS DEMAND TRANSPARENCY, NOT SUSPICION

Former Election Commissioner Ashok Lavasa has raised serious concerns about the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls in West Bengal. Speaking at a citizens’ convention on 13 October, he alleged that voters were being removed on suspicion about their citizenship rather than on the basis of sufficient evidence.

According to The Wire's report, Lavasa also alleged that Electoral Registration Officers (EROs)—the officials legally authorised to delete names—were denied access to the Election Commission's centrally controlled ECINET software. He questioned the legality and fairness of a system in which officials responsible for electoral rolls may not have effective access to the tools needed to discharge their statutory duties.

These are serious allegations from a former Election Commissioner. They demand a clear, evidence-based response from the Election Commission.

THE APPEALS FIGURES RAISE ANOTHER IMPORTANT QUESTION

According to figures from an Election Commission report submitted to the Supreme Court, approximately 38.3 lakh appeals relating to SIR in West Bengal were filed before tribunals:

- 22.2 lakh appeals concerned voters excluded from the rolls who sought relief.
- 16.1 lakh appeals challenged the inclusion of voters whose names had been retained or restored.

These figures do not, by themselves, prove that every deletion was wrongful or that the entire process was politically motivated. But they demonstrate the enormous scale of the dispute and the need for transparent, independently scrutinizable decisions.

When an eligible citizen's name is removed, the consequences are not merely administrative. That person may lose the practical ability to exercise the constitutional right to vote.

THE QUESTIONS THE ECI MUST ANSWER

1. Were all deletions supported by individualised evidence and the procedures required by law?
2. Did authorised Electoral Registration Officers retain the powers and system access necessary to make lawful decisions?
3. Why are so many cases being contested before appellate tribunals?
4. How many excluded voters have been restored, how many exclusions have been upheld, and on what grounds?
5. What effective safeguards ensure that poor people, migrants, elderly citizens and people lacking extensive documentation are not unfairly excluded?

The Election Commission must publish clear, verifiable, category-wise data and explain the safeguards used to prevent wrongful deletion.

THE PRINCIPLE IS SIMPLE: CLEAN ELECTORAL ROLLS MUST NOT COME AT THE COST OF ELIGIBLE VOTERS.

The objective of accurate voter lists is legitimate. Removing deceased persons and genuine duplicate entries matters. But suspicion, a database discrepancy or an administrative mismatch should not replace a fair procedure grounded in evidence and law.

Every eligible voter must have a meaningful opportunity to establish eligibility, challenge an erroneous deletion and obtain timely relief before an election.

Demanding answers from the Election Commission is not an attack on democracy. It is a demand that a constitutional institution fulfil its responsibility to protect the integrity of the electoral process—and every eligible citizen's right to participate in it.

NO WRONGFUL DELETION. NO ARBITRARY EXCLUSION. NO SELECTIVE ACCOUNTABILITY.

Let the evidence be examined impartially. Let the Commission answer legitimate questions transparently. Where violations are established, accountability must follow.

OUR DEMOCRACY MUST COUNT EVERY ELIGIBLE VOTER—NOT MAKE CITIZENS FIGHT FOR THE RIGHT TO BE COUNTED.

MeitY's advisory to Meta directs the suppression of protest reporting on Instagram and Facebook. It must be withdrawn.

19 Oct 2026

On 10 October 2026, the Cyber Laws Division of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology issued an advisory to Meta Platforms bearing File No. 6(2)/2026-Cyberlaws. It was not published on the MEITY website and first HT and then PTI reported it on 18 October. Any such advisory is not a legal order and MEITY is not legally empowered to issue them on the basis of any statutory provision. This advisory followed, by two days, an advisory of 8 October to all social media intermediaries calling for "enhanced diligence" over content on "ongoing public events", asking platforms to "label or add context" to misleading content and to "give priority to complaints from authorised Government agencies".  IFF called for the withdrawal of that advisory on 9 October. The Meta advisory was issued on the day the Delhi Police detained protesters and journalists at the demonstrations called over the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls.

The advisory states that content relating to "public-order and law and order situations" is being "prominently displayed and recommended" on Meta's platforms and, "when presented without adequate context or disproportionately amplified", "may contribute to public confusion, apprehension and disturbance of public order and social tranquillity". It singles out "unverified or misleading claims regarding the imposition of emergency, restrictions, police action or other official measures". Further, Meta is advised to review its "recommendation and content ranking mechanisms", to ensure its systems "do not result in disproportionate exposure of users to a single or limited set of narratives", and to furnish "information or assistance" to law enforcement, "with immediate effect". PTI reports that the Ministry acted on inputs from "agencies" that Meta's platforms were not promoting all "narratives" equally.

This advisory matches restrictions on META platforms related to protest content and reporting in the same timline. On 10 October, the Instagram account of Molitics India was withheld in India. On 11 October, a Mathrubhumi English reel showing a woman clinging to a pole as police officers attempted to detain her was restricted citing, "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement", and a video report by Observer Post Hindi was restricted on Facebook by what Meta called an "automated system" acting under the IT Rules, 2021. On 12 October, the Instagram account of journalist Shubhangi Das Gupta was restricted in India for alleged non-compliance with "local IT Rules". On 13 October, the account of Journo Mirror (about five lakh followers) was withheld. The account of Fridays For Future India has since been withheld without any stated reason. Meta's notices to these users do not disclose what is unlawful about the content. 

As per notices shared by us by those who have been censored by META, they take two forms: 

1. "a notice from the Government of India/Law Enforcement under Section 79(3)(b)", and, 

2. "through an automated system implemented pursuant to legal requirements under India's Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules". 

Neither names the issuing agency, the order, the provision of law or offence the content is said to disclose, or the URL complained of. We know due to litigation that the first notice related to a Sahyog order issued by a Law Enforcement Agency (LEA), while the second one is without any legal order. At the same time, several users received no communication at all. Instagram used the same "automated system" notice against Anjali Priya, Varnika Dhawan and Sachin Gupta after the July protests, and against cartoonist Satish Acharya, who lost nine cartoons and then his account between February and September 2026. 

In April 2026, The Hindu reported that Meta automatically restricts government and police flagged content in India at scale, and seeks a separate government direction before restoring content later found to be legally unsupported. IFF objected to Meta on 4 May 2026. IFF condemns the advisory of 10 October and the restrictions imposed in its wake. An executive communication that instructs a platform to suppress "unverified" claims about "police action" and to correct a "limited set of narratives", issued on the day of a police crackdown and kept from the public, is a censorship directive in all but name.  It makes the State the editor of what Indians may see of a protest against the State. IFF calls upon MeitY to withdraw it and upon Meta to disclose what it has done under it.

Our demands

1. MeitY must withdraw the advisories of 8 and 10 October 2026 forthwith and publish them.

2. MeitY must abandon proposed Rule 3(4) and restrict content only by reasoned, published orders under Section 69A or notices compliant with Rule 3(1)(d).

3. Meta must disclose every takedown, account restriction and act of downranking carried out under the advisories, and its compliance report to the Ministry.

4. Meta must restore the accounts and posts of journalists, outlets and creators restricted since 8 October 2026 unless it holds a valid legal order, and must furnish that order to the person affected.

5. Meta must suspend the automated restriction of content in India and disclose on what inputs its "automated system" acts.

Any person whose account or content has been withheld in India since 8 October 2026 may write to IFF at legal@internetfreedom.in. IFF is providing assistance pro bono.

WHEN A CREATOR SPEAKS UP, DOES HER VOICE BECOME THE TARGET? DIGITAL CENSORSHIP, META RESTRICTIONS AND THE RIGHT TO BE HEARD

A creator behind @the.ranting.gola has shared a disturbing account of restrictions on her Facebook activity. In her video, she says she cannot go LIVE for a year, send messages, post videos to her broadcast group or share videos to her Story. She also describes monetisation being unavailable and some content becoming inaccessible in India.

She says she had made a video supporting Neha Singh Rathore and opposing ABVP-related groups. According to her account, she was not clearly informed which specific post had triggered the restrictions and had to investigate the matter herself.

These are the creator’s allegations and account of her experience. The precise reason for the restrictions, the applicable Meta policy and whether a government direction was involved have not been independently established from this video alone.

But her experience raises a fundamental democratic question: What happens when ordinary citizens and independent creators lose their ability to communicate with their audiences without receiving a clear explanation?

THIS IS NOT AN ISOLATED CONCERN

Recent reporting in India makes these questions particularly urgent.

• ThePrint, 19 October 2026: Reported on a MeitY advisory asking Meta to review its Facebook and Instagram recommendation systems, alongside restrictions affecting posts and accounts connected with protests and political events.

https://t.co/QeWUIIrGmC

• Alt News, 15 October 2026: Documented restrictions affecting journalists and media organisations covering the Delhi protests, including cases in which Meta notices cited automated enforcement or government and law-enforcement requests.

https://t.co/1RjkoJX1nE

• Reporters Without Borders: Reported a broader rise in restrictions affecting journalistic content in India during 2026, raising concerns about opaque takedown processes and the public’s right to information.

https://t.co/g6FhmAUglC

These reports provide important context. They do not, by themselves, establish that this particular creator was restricted at the government's request. That question deserves a direct, evidence-based answer.

THE REAL ISSUE: TRANSPARENCY AND ACCOUNTABILITY

Social media companies have the right to enforce legitimate community standards. But enforcement must be proportionate, transparent and open to meaningful appeal.

If a creator is prohibited from going LIVE for an entire year, the platform should explain:

Which specific post, video or action triggered the restriction?
Which rule was allegedly violated, and what evidence supports that decision?
Was the action taken under Meta's own policies, an automated system or a government/legal request?
Why were such extensive restrictions imposed, and what appeal and restoration mechanisms are available?

A vague account-status notification is not an adequate substitute for a meaningful explanation.

DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY ELECTIONS

Democracy also depends on the freedom to question power, criticise political organisations, support dissenting voices and share information without arbitrary punishment.

Statement : Shutting down Telegram is a band aid solution and is a disproportionate answer to exam fraud

The Internet Freedom Foundation objects to the directions announced today in the National Testing Agency's press release on action against the Telegram platform. On the NTA's recommendation, the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology has, under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, restricted access to the whole of Telegram in India until 22 June 2026, and has separately ordered the platform to switch off message-editing for every Indian user until 30 June 2026. This is a blunt, nationwide measure aimed at the conduct of rampant fraud rackets, and on the Government's own admission is constitutionally incompatible.

At the outset it is important to note that Section 69A and the Blocking Rules of 2009 framed under it allow the Government to block access to specific “information” on a computer resource. They do not extend to switching off an entire intermediary, still less to ordering a company to redesign its product by removing a feature for a whole country. In Shreya Singhal v Union of India, the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A because it is narrow and hedged with procedural safeguards. Reading it to authorise shutting down a platform that lakhs use is an overbroad restriction by the NTAs own admission. For the message-editing direction the release identifies no source of power at all. If one exists, the order must say so.

The release argues against itself

A restriction on access has to be the least intrusive measure that achieves its aim as per the constitutional test of proportionality laid down in Justice K.S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017) and applied in Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020). The NTA's own narration shows the block fails its nodal agency, the release says, “has secured the prompt take-down of a substantial number of Telegram channels, groups and bots”, and this targeted work “is the reason the harm caused by these rackets has been contained to the extent it has”. If channel level takedown contained the harm, the case for a blanket block collapses and hence the Government has reached for a heavier tool while conceding that a lighter one was working. The collateral cost sits on the record too as noted in the press release. The block, the NTA accepts, “affects lakhs of citizens who use the Telegram platform for legitimate personal, educational, professional and informational purposes”. The release also says there is "no such paper available outside the secured examination chain" and that “the security of the examination is unaffected by the action taken”. If the exam is secure and no leak exists, what is being suppressed is rumour, and rumour cannot justify closing a platform when specific blocking and criminal prosecution remain available.

Students use of Telegram

The block of telegram is reactive and ineffective and will punish ordinary users instead of addressing the systemic source of exam leaks. This blocking comes in the final days of NEET preparation, when thousands of students depend on Telegram for study groups, doubt-clearing, and shared resources. Also, it is important to consider that the source of exam papers leak will occur from inside the system, among insiders and across the printing and logistics chain, with the platform being the most downstream channel for distribution. Hence, switching off Telegram, is merely a deflection from the repeated failures that will continue while media attention is directed towards this Telegram ban.

Lack of transparency

At present only a press release from the NTA has been provided, which recommended the block but the reasoned order of MeitY, the authority that issued it, has not been released. The Anuradha Bhasin decision requires that orders restricting access be published so they can be tested in court. Here the order, and the reasoning of the committee behind it, stay out of view, and we do not know whether Telegram was heard at all. An announcement of a block is no substitute for an order the affected party can challenge.
Blunt to enforce and very easy to evade
Usually, app-level blocks run through IS-level DNS and IP filtering. They are over inclusive, sweeping in lawful use, yet simple to evade as a determined exam leak racket moves to a VPN or a mirror within minutes while ordinary users lose the service for a week.

We ask the Government to:

1) Publish the MeitY Section 69A order and the NTA recommendation behind it, with reasons;
2) State the legal basis for the message editing direction, or withdraw it;
3) Confirm whether Telegram was given a hearing under the Blocking Rules, and place the committee's record before any court that hears a challenge; and
4) Lift the platform-wide restriction and rely on the targeted takedowns the NTA itself credits with containing the harm.

We emphasise that the NEET (UG) 2026 re-examination is worth protecting and it concerns the future of lakhs of aspirants. It requires securing the entire process of examination rather than reaching for purported band aid solutions that instead cause more harm. The State cannot switch off a service used by lakhs to answer the wrongdoing of a few, and cannot do it through an order no one affected is allowed to read. On its own facts, the Government has done both.

These reports demand answers: What were the legal grounds for each detention? Were seized devices returned? Were allegations of excessive force independently investigated?

Alt News documented restrictions on posts by opposition organisations, political leaders and creators, including content associated with the Cockroach Janata Party protests. The Indian Express separately reported that government blocking orders increased during the period of student protests.

The central issue is whether restrictions are lawful, necessary, proportionate and open to meaningful challenge. The government and platforms should disclose the legal basis for restrictions to the extent permitted by law and provide effective remedies against erroneous takedowns.

4. MEDIA OWNERSHIP AND CORPORATE INFLUENCE

India's media ownership is concentrated among powerful corporate groups, raising legitimate questions about editorial independence, conflicts of interest and the influence of commercial interests on public debate.

But ownership alone does not prove that every newsroom follows government instructions. Each allegation of editorial interference should be supported by evidence.

5. WHY NO REGULAR SOLO PRESS CONFERENCES?

Reuters reported in May 2019 that Narendra Modi attended a press conference but did not take questions, directing a journalist to then BJP president Amit Shah instead. The absence of regular, open question-and-answer press conferences has therefore become a legitimate subject of democratic scrutiny.

A prime minister should be willing to face difficult questions from independent journalists. Interviews and public speeches are not substitutes for sustained, open questioning.

6. WHAT ABOUT BOTS AND COORDINATED ONLINE HARASSMENT?

The video alleges that fake accounts and bots systematically attack critics and defend the government. Such coordination is possible, but this particular allegation needs account-level evidence, platform investigations or credible independent research before it can be treated as established fact.

Do not confuse an allegation with a proven finding. Demand the evidence.

THE DEMOCRATIC TEST IS SIMPLE:

- Can journalists investigate those in power without intimidation?
- Can citizens criticise government policy without arbitrary censorship?
- Can peaceful protesters document events and share evidence?
- Can platforms explain why content was removed and offer meaningful appeals?
- Can the Prime Minister face unscripted questions from the press?

These are not demands for privilege. They are demands for transparency and accountability in a constitutional democracy.

The government may legitimately restrict unlawful content and maintain public order. But those powers must not become a shield against scrutiny or a means of suppressing peaceful dissent.

A DEMOCRACY CANNOT BE MEASURED ONLY BY THE ELECTIONS IT HOLDS. IT MUST ALSO BE MEASURED BY THE QUESTIONS ITS LEADERS ARE WILLING TO ANSWER.

Verify the evidence. Challenge censorship. Defend independent journalism. Protect the right to dissent.

text: Narendra Modi employs the oldest and most tried-and-true political trick in the book to maintain control of media outlets and shape the dominant narrative. The government has used 195,000 social media takedown orders to systematically suppress online content and voices. Journalists have been detained and prevented from freely reporting, and the Prime Minister has strategically avoided holding solo press conferences where he could be questioned directly. Throughout this process, accountability mechanisms have been deliberately dismantled and destroyed, effectively silencing opposition voices and preventing meaningful dissent from reaching the public sphere.

ONE GOVERNMENT BLOCKING ORDER EVERY 68 SECONDS — IS INDIA'S DIGITAL DEMOCRACY UNDER THREAT?

Pause for a moment. In the five months from March to July 2026, nearly 1.95 lakh government-backed blocking orders were sent to Instagram, Facebook and YouTube, according to data reported by The Indian Express.

That is approximately 1,275 orders every day. One every 68 seconds.

This is not a trivial administrative statistic. It raises a fundamental democratic question: who decides what citizens are allowed to see, discuss and criticise online?

🚨 THE NUMBERS DEMAND PUBLIC SCRUTINY

* Instagram received nearly 1 lakh orders.

* Facebook received around 80,000.

* YouTube received nearly 15,000.

* Meta's two platforms—Instagram and Facebook—accounted for roughly nine out of every ten orders directed to these three platforms.

For comparison, RTI information previously reported by The Indian Express showed 2,312 blocking orders sent through the Sahyog portal to 19 platforms between October 2024 and October 2025.

The scale of the subsequent increase deserves a detailed public explanation.

THE MOST DISTURBING QUESTION: CAN A MACHINE REMOVE OUR VOICE WITHOUT MEANINGFUL HUMAN REVIEW?

According to The Indian Express, Meta integrated its API with the government's Sahyog portal to comply with a shortened takedown deadline. The report says this enabled government-flagged content to be removed automatically, without a separate human review by the company.

Automation may make administration faster. But speed is not the same as justice.

What happens if an order is mistaken, overbroad or insufficiently justified? Who checks whether the content actually violates the law? How quickly can an ordinary citizen challenge the decision and restore lawful speech?

A system that can silence first and explain later needs exceptionally strong safeguards.

📢 WHY THIS MATTERS TO EVERY CITIZEN

The reported orders coincided with student protests against examination-paper leaks at Delhi's Jantar Mantar. The reporting also described takedowns affecting posts concerning the government's ethanol-blending policy and the West Bengal elections.

The presence of a takedown order does not, by itself, prove unlawful censorship. Governments have legitimate duties to address unlawful content, and the law permits restrictions in defined circumstances.

But criticism of the government, peaceful protest, investigative journalism and political disagreement must not be casually treated as threats merely because they are uncomfortable for those in power.

India's constitutional commitment to freedom of speech cannot survive on assurances alone. It requires lawful orders, transparent procedures, independent scrutiny and effective remedies.

⚖️ THE LAW MUST NOT BECOME A SHORTCUT AROUND DUE PROCESS

The reporting distinguishes the takedown mechanism associated with Section 79(3)(b) of the Information Technology Act from the separate blocking framework under Section 69A.

These are not interchangeable provisions. Their legal basis, procedures and safeguards matter. The public deserves clarity about which authority issued each order, what legal grounds were invoked and what opportunity affected users had to challenge it.

OUR DEMANDS

1. Publish regular, platform-wise statistics on government takedown orders, their legal grounds and their outcomes.
2. Ensure meaningful human and legal review of disputed or ambiguous directions.
3. Give affected users clear notice, subject to narrowly justified exceptions, and an effective appeal mechanism.
4. Disclose the safeguards governing automated integration between government portals and social-media platforms.
5. Ensure that peaceful dissent, journalism and legitimate political criticism are not suppressed through vague or overbroad directions.
6. Enable independent judicial scrutiny wherever legality or fundamental rights are contested.

India cannot call itself the world's largest democracy while treating transparency about restrictions on public speech as optional.

THE ISSUE IS NOT WHETHER GOVERNMENTS CAN ENFORCE THE LAW. THE ISSUE IS WHETHER THEY CAN DO SO WITHOUT ACCOUNTABILITY.

A democracy must protect citizens from unlawful content—but it must also protect citizens' right to question the state.

When posts disappear, citizens deserve to know why. When orders are issued, the public deserves to know under what authority. And when lawful speech is wrongly removed, there must be a meaningful remedy.

Digital India must not become a system in which technology makes silencing citizens easier than answering them.

→ So I went to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, 2021, X must appoint a Resident Grievance Officer in India. He has no email address. X does not accept legal notices by email. 

The only options are a web form or post to their physical office.

Here's what worked:

→First, a cyber complaint on https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW (or call 1930).

→Second, a legal notice to the Grievance Officer. Under the IT Rules, impersonation complaints must be acted on within 24 hours.

→Third, the same notice sent by registered post, and to every X email address I could find.

The notice put X on record. It set out the ticket number, the phishing link, and the cyber complaint number. It showed proof of ownership: the registered email, the phone number, and the Premium subscription paid from my card. It ended with a clear ask and a deadline.

Six days after the hack, I was back in.

If this happens to you:
• Act within hours
• File X's hacked account form from your registered email and be persistent (this is important)
• File at https://t.co/Uzds8BObDW and keep the acknowledgement
• Notice to the Grievance Officer via the https://t.co/YkDfcMQwzE form and by post

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

2. The direction must be withdrawn. Any specific unlawful use must be met with targeted proceedings under due process, not the removal of a communications tool for everyone.

3. Apple must disclose the demand in its transparency reporting and notify its users in India, and must state whether parallel directions have been received in respect of other app stores.

4. The secrecy of the blocking regime must end. The Blocking Rules, 2009 should be amended to require publication of orders and notice to originators, without awaiting the outcome of the pending constitutional challenge.

The Internet Freedom Foundation will file applications under the Right to Information Act seeking a copy of the order, and stands ready to assist the developers and affected users in India.
